title: Practice Set PRS3 — Plan Stability Across Versions
description: Senior applied-architecture track: diff plans across Spark versions, identify which plan needs pinning. Companion to PSS2 advanced AQE internals.

datasets.description: Schema reference (sample rows). Senior plan-reading scenarios describe GridUnion Continental at platform scale (850M meters across 4 countries, 30 regions, 6 teams, 8TB+ archive); the CSV itself is a small sample for schema reference.
Substations reference. Anchors cross-team architectural scenarios.

tasks.title: Plan Diff Across Spark Versions

description.context: GridUnion is upgrading from Spark 3.4.2 to Spark 3.5.1. The architect runs the upgrade-validation suite which prints plan diffs for each pipeline. One window-function plan changed in a way that broke a SLA-critical pipeline's plan-stability test. The change is benign for most pipelines, but this one pipeline hard-coded the old operator name 'WindowExec' in its plan-stability assertion; the new name is 'RunningWindowFunctionExec'. The architect reads the diff and decides what to do.
description.task: What is the right interpretation of this plan diff?

evidence.title: Input sample
evidence.content:
Spark 3 4 Operator: WindowExec

Spark 3 5 Operator: RunningWindowFunctionExec

Rewrite Introduced In: SPARK-43284 (Spark 3.5)

Affected Pipeline: Risk team's portfolio-aging window-function query

Plan Stability Test Assertion: expects exactly the string 'WindowExec' in printed plan

Result Correctness Unchanged: true (output rows identical)

evidence.title: Dataset
evidence.content: Plan diff between Spark 3.4 and 3.5 showing a Catalyst rewrite that renames a window-function operator

evidence.label: Plan output
evidence.content:
# Plan diff (Spark 3.4 → 3.5)

  +- HashAggregate(keys=[counterparty_id], functions=[sum(exposure)])
     +- Project [counterparty_id, exposure, age_bucket]
-       +- WindowExec [row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY counterparty_id ORDER BY trade_date)]
+       +- RunningWindowFunctionExec [row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY counterparty_id ORDER BY trade_date)]
           +- Sort [counterparty_id ASC, trade_date ASC NULLS FIRST]
              +- Exchange hashpartitioning(counterparty_id, 800)
                 +- FileScan parquet positions

# Test assertion that broke:
#   plan_text = df.queryExecution.executedPlan.toString
#   assert 'WindowExec' in plan_text  ← fails on 3.5 because operator renamed

# Correctness check:
#   df_3_4.collect() == df_3_5.collect()  ← passes; same output rows

fields.label: What is the right interpretation of this plan diff?
options: The plan diff signals a regression in Spark 3.5; the WindowExec operator was the standard name for years and should not have been renamed. Response: file an upstream Spark bug and pin the cluster to 3.4 until the rename is reverted.

The diff invalidates the upgrade entirely; if any plan changes, the upgrade is unsafe. Response: roll back to Spark 3.4 cluster-wide and audit which other pipelines have stability tests that would break.

The diff means Spark 3.5 introduced a new physical operator that runs slower for window functions; output rows are correct but performance degraded. Response: disable the new operator via spark.sql.windowExec.legacy=true.

The diff is benign at the result level (output rows identical) but breaks plan-stability assertions written against operator names. Response: update the test assertion to match either operator name OR pin the plan via QUERY hint.
fields.correctAnswer: The diff is benign at the result level (output rows identical) but breaks plan-stability assertions written against operator names. Response: update the test assertion to match either operator name OR pin the plan via QUERY hint.
fields.rationale: Plan diffs across Spark versions are common and usually benign — Catalyst evolves continuously.
fields.distractorRationale: Option A: Treats rename as regression; renames are normal Catalyst evolution.

tasks.pssReference: PSS2 lesson 9 (Plan Stability Across Spark Versions), PSS9 lesson 7 (Upgrade Risk Assessment).

tasks.title: Which Plan Needs Pinning?

description.context: GridUnion's architect runs the Spark 3.5 upgrade-validation suite against three SLA-critical queries. Q1's plan is identical across versions. Q2's plan changed (operator rename only) but output is identical. Q3's plan changed in a way that affects partitioning — the new plan uses a different shuffle hashpartitioning and a downstream consumer pipeline depends on partition layout for incremental processing. The architect must classify which need plan pinning, which need stability tests only, and which can drift freely.
description.task: Which classification is correct for each query?

evidence.title: Input sample
evidence.content:
Q1 Status: Plan identical 3.4 → 3.5; output identical

Q2 Status: Plan changed (operator rename); output identical; downstream consumers don't read partition layout

Q3 Status: Plan changed (different hashpartitioning); output identical at row level BUT partitions are arranged differently; downstream incremental pipeline reads partition_id to skip processed partitions

evidence.title: Dataset
evidence.content: Three SLA-critical queries with three different plan-stability profiles across a Spark version upgrade

evidence.label: Plan output
evidence.content:
# Q1: identical plan, identical output → no concern

# Q2: operator rename only
-   +- WindowExec [row_number() ...]
+   +- RunningWindowFunctionExec [row_number() ...]
#   downstream: Reporting team's daily summary; reads result rows only

# Q3: hashpartitioning function changed
-   +- Exchange hashpartitioning(meter_id, 800), MURMUR3
+   +- Exchange hashpartitioning(meter_id, 800), XXHASH64
#   downstream: Compaction team's incremental pipeline reads partition_id
#               and skips partitions that haven't changed
#   change effect: every partition_id is now different;
#                  Compaction's 'changed since last run' logic
#                  treats EVERY partition as new and reprocesses 100% of data

# Architecture decision: classify each query's pinning requirement

fields.label: Which classification is correct for each query?
options: All three need plan pinning. Any plan change in production is risky regardless of downstream behavior; pinning provides safety margin and consistency across teams. Response: pin Q1, Q2, Q3 with explicit query hints.

None of the three need action. SLA-critical queries are 'critical' for output correctness, not plan structure. As long as df.collect() returns identical rows, plan changes are irrelevant. Response: nothing.
Q1 needs no action. Q2 needs an updated stability test (assert structural properties not operator names). Q3 needs plan pinning OR a downstream contract not depending on hash function.
Q1 and Q2 need pinning to prevent future drift across Spark upgrades. Q3 needs to be rewritten to remove the window function which is causing the underlying instability across versions.
fields.correctAnswer: Q1 needs no action. Q2 needs an updated stability test (assert structural properties not operator names). Q3 needs plan pinning OR a downstream contract not depending on hash function.
fields.rationale: Senior architecture distinguishes three classes.Q1 has no problem and no action needed.
fields.distractorRationale: Option A: Treats all plan changes as equally risky; produces upgrade paralysis.

tasks.pssReference: PSS2 lesson 9 (Plan Stability), PSS9 lesson 8 (Pipeline Contracts and Partition Layout).
